There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah— Genesis 49:31 the field and the cave that is in it were bought from the Hittites.” Genesis 49:32 When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people. Genesis 49:33

title: Genesis 5:1–20
context: After Cain’s line in chapter 4, Genesis 5 opens the “book of the generations of Adam”—image-bearing humanity named Man, then the Sethite succession marching toward Noah. The refrain “and he died” sounds the curse after Eden; the long years still display God’s patience preserving a people.
text: Genesis 5:1–20 Genesis After Cain’s line in chapter 4, Genesis 5 opens the “book of the generations of Adam”—image-bearing humanity named Man, then the Sethite succession marching toward Noah. The refrain “and he died” sounds the curse after Eden; the long years still display God’s patience preserving a people. This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Genesis 5:1 Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created. Genesis 5:2 When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. Genesis 5:3 The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:4 Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died. Genesis 5:5 When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh. Genesis 5:6 Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:7 Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died. Genesis 5:8 When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan. Genesis 5:9 Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:10 Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died. Genesis 5:11 When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel. Genesis 5:12 Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:13 Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died. Genesis 5:14 When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared. Genesis 5:15 Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:16 Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died. Genesis 5:17 When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch. Genesis 5:18 Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:19 Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died. Genesis 5:20

title: Genesis 5:21–32
context: The genealogy breaks its death-refrain for Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. Methuselah’s long life, Lamech’s naming of Noah as hoped relief from the cursed ground, and Noah’s three sons then carry the line God will preserve through the flood.
text: Genesis 5:21–32 Genesis The genealogy breaks its death-refrain for Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. Methuselah’s long life, Lamech’s naming of Noah as hoped relief from the cursed ground, and Noah’s three sons then carry the line God will preserve through the flood. When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah. Genesis 5:21 Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:22 Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years. Genesis 5:23 Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. Genesis 5:24 When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech. Genesis 5:25 Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:26 Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died. Genesis 5:27 When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son Genesis 5:28 and called his name Noah, saying, “Out of the ground that the Lord has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands.” Genesis 5:29 Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:30 Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died. Genesis 5:31 After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Genesis 5:32

title: Genesis 50:1–14
context: Joseph weeps over Jacob, has Israel embalmed, and Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave a great company goes up to Canaan, laments at Atad, and buries him in Machpelah—Abraham’s purchased cave—then Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt.
text: Genesis 50:1–14 Genesis Joseph weeps over Jacob, has Israel embalmed, and Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave a great company goes up to Canaan, laments at Atad, and buries him in Machpelah—Abraham’s purchased cave—then Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt. Then Joseph fell on his father’s face and wept over him and kissed him. Genesis 50:1 And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel. Genesis 50:2 Forty days were required for it, for that is how many are required for embalming. And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days. Genesis 50:3 And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying, Genesis 50:4 ‘My father made me swear, saying, “I am about to die: in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there shall you bury me.” Now therefore, let me please go up and bury my father. Then I will return.’” Genesis 50:5 And Pharaoh answered, “Go up, and bury your father, as he made you swear.” Genesis 50:6 So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, Genesis 50:7 as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left in the land of Goshen. Genesis 50:8 And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company. Genesis 50:9 When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he made a mourning for his father seven days. Genesis 50:10 When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan. Genesis 50:11 Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them, Genesis 50:12 for his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. Genesis 50:13 After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father. Genesis 50:14

title: Genesis 50:15–26
context: After Jacob’s burial, Joseph’s brothers fear that with their father gone he will finally repay the evil they did. They send a plea for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place, and reads the sale through providence: they meant evil, God meant it for good, that many people should live. He provides for them, lives 110 years, and dies in Egypt under oath that God will visit them and that his bones will go up—hope aimed at the Exodus.
text: Genesis 50:15–26 Genesis After Jacob’s burial, Joseph’s brothers fear that with their father gone he will finally repay the evil they did. They send a plea for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place, and reads the sale through providence: they meant evil, God meant it for good, that many people should live. He provides for them, lives 110 years, and dies in Egypt under oath that God will visit them and that his bones will go up—hope aimed at the Exodus. When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him.” Genesis 50:15 So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father gave this command before he died: Genesis 50:16 ‘Say to Joseph, “Please forgive the transgression of your brothers and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ And now, please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him. Genesis 50:17 His brothers also came and fell down before him and said, “Behold, we are your servants.” Genesis 50:18 But Joseph said to them, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? Genesis 50:19 As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. Genesis 50:20 So do not fear; I will provide for you and your little ones.” Thus he comforted them and spoke kindly to them. Genesis 50:21 So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father’s house. Joseph lived 110 years. Genesis 50:22 And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were counted as Joseph’s own. Genesis 50:23 And Joseph said to his brothers, “I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” Genesis 50:24 Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.” Genesis 50:25 So Joseph died, being 110 years old. They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt. Genesis 50:26

title: Genesis 6:1–8
context: As humanity multiplies, boundaries blur and violence ripens. The Lord limits His Spirit’s striving with flesh, names the earth’s great wickedness—every intention only evil continually—and grieves to His heart. Judgment is announced: He will blot out man and creature from the land. Yet the dark paragraph ends with a door: Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.
text: Genesis 6:1–8 Genesis As humanity multiplies, boundaries blur and violence ripens. The Lord limits His Spirit’s striving with flesh, names the earth’s great wickedness—every intention only evil continually—and grieves to His heart. Judgment is announced: He will blot out man and creature from the land. Yet the dark paragraph ends with a door: Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord. When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, Genesis 6:1 the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose. Genesis 6:2 Then the Lord said, “My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years.” Genesis 6:3 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown. Genesis 6:4 The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. Genesis 6:5 And the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart. Genesis 6:6 So the Lord said, “I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them.” Genesis 6:7 But Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord. Genesis 6:8

title: Genesis 6:9–22
context: A new toledoth names Noah: righteous, blameless in his generation, a man who walked with God. The earth is corrupt and violent; God tells Noah He will end all flesh and commands an ark—precise, pitched, three-decked—then pledges covenant, a household inside, and pairs of living things preserved. Noah does all that God commanded him.
text: Genesis 6:9–22 Genesis A new toledoth names Noah: righteous, blameless in his generation, a man who walked with God. The earth is corrupt and violent; God tells Noah He will end all flesh and commands an ark—precise, pitched, three-decked—then pledges covenant, a household inside, and pairs of living things preserved. Noah does all that God commanded him. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. Genesis 6:9 And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Genesis 6:10 Now the earth was corrupt in God’s sight, and the earth was filled with violence. Genesis 6:11 And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth. Genesis 6:12 And God said to Noah, “I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth. Genesis 6:13 Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch. Genesis 6:14 This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. Genesis 6:15 Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks. Genesis 6:16 For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die. Genesis 6:17 But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. Genesis 6:18 And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Genesis 6:19 Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive. Genesis 6:20 Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them.” Genesis 6:21 Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him. Genesis 6:22

title: Genesis 7:1–16
context: The LORD commands Noah to go into the ark with his household, for He has seen him righteous in this generation, and to take clean and unclean animals and birds so that offspring will live. In seven days rain will fall forty days and nights and blot out every living thing. Noah obeys. At six hundred years he and his family enter; after seven days the flood comes. On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open; they enter two by two of all flesh, and the LORD shuts him in.
text: Genesis 7:1–16 Genesis The LORD commands Noah to go into the ark with his household, for He has seen him righteous in this generation, and to take clean and unclean animals and birds so that offspring will live. In seven days rain will fall forty days and nights and blot out every living thing. Noah obeys. At six hundred years he and his family enter; after seven days the flood comes. On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open; they enter two by two of all flesh, and the LORD shuts him in. Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation." Genesis 7:1 Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate, Genesis 7:2 and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth. Genesis 7:3 For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground." Genesis 7:4 And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him. Genesis 7:5 Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth. Genesis 7:6 And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood. Genesis 7:7 Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground, Genesis 7:8 two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah. Genesis 7:9 And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth. Genesis 7:10 In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. Genesis 7:11 And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights. Genesis 7:12 On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark, Genesis 7:13 they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature. Genesis 7:14 They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life. Genesis 7:15 And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in. Genesis 7:16

title: Genesis 7:17–24
context: Judgment falls as the Lord had said: waters increase forty days, lift the ark high above the earth, and cover even the high mountains. All flesh that moved on dry land dies—everything with the breath of life. God blots out every living thing on the ground; only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters prevail 150 days.
text: Genesis 7:17–24 Genesis Judgment falls as the Lord had said: waters increase forty days, lift the ark high above the earth, and cover even the high mountains. All flesh that moved on dry land dies—everything with the breath of life. God blots out every living thing on the ground; only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters prevail 150 days. The flood continued forty days on the earth. The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth. Genesis 7:17 The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters. Genesis 7:18 And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. Genesis 7:19 The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep. Genesis 7:20 And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind. Genesis 7:21 Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died. Genesis 7:22 He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark. Genesis 7:23 And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days. Genesis 7:24

title: Genesis 8:1–19
context: After the flood, God remembers Noah and the creatures in the ark; the waters recede, the ark rests on Ararat, and Noah waits with raven and dove until God commands the family and the animals to go out and fill the earth again.
text: Genesis 8:1–19 Genesis After the flood, God remembers Noah and the creatures in the ark; the waters recede, the ark rests on Ararat, and Noah waits with raven and dove until God commands the family and the animals to go out and fill the earth again. But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided. Genesis 8:1 The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained, Genesis 8:2 and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated, Genesis 8:3 and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Genesis 8:4 And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen. Genesis 8:5 At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made Genesis 8:6 and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth. Genesis 8:7 Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground. Genesis 8:8 But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him. Genesis 8:9 He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark. Genesis 8:10 And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth. Genesis 8:11 Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore. Genesis 8:12 In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry. Genesis 8:13 In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out. Genesis 8:14 Then God said to Noah, Genesis 8:15 “Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons’ wives with you.” Genesis 8:16 “Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth.” Genesis 8:17 So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons’ wives with him. Genesis 8:18 Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark. Genesis 8:19

title: Genesis 8:20–22
context: Noah’s first act on dry ground is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings; the LORD smells the pleasing aroma and promises never again to curse the ground or strike down every living creature as in the flood, while earth’s seasons endure.
text: Genesis 8:20–22 Genesis Noah’s first act on dry ground is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings; the LORD smells the pleasing aroma and promises never again to curse the ground or strike down every living creature as in the flood, while earth’s seasons endure. Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. Genesis 8:20 And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, “I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done.” Genesis 8:21 While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease. Genesis 8:22

title: Genesis 9:1–17
context: After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, restores the call to fill the earth, sets limits around blood and human life, and establishes a covenant with all flesh—signed by the bow in the clouds—that a flood will never again destroy the earth.
text: Genesis 9:1–17 Genesis After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, restores the call to fill the earth, sets limits around blood and human life, and establishes a covenant with all flesh—signed by the bow in the clouds—that a flood will never again destroy the earth. And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. Genesis 9:1 The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered. Genesis 9:2 Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything. Genesis 9:3 But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood. Genesis 9:4 And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. Genesis 9:5 “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. Genesis 9:6 And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it.” Genesis 9:7 Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, Genesis 9:8 “Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you, Genesis 9:9 and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth. Genesis 9:10 I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth.” Genesis 9:11 And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: Genesis 9:12 I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. Genesis 9:13 When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, Genesis 9:14 I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. Genesis 9:15 When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.” Genesis 9:16 God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.” Genesis 9:17

title: Genesis 9:18–29
context: Noah’s three sons go forth from the ark to people the earth; then the rescued patriarch plants a vineyard, falls in shameful drunkenness, and a family crisis ends in curse on Canaan and blessing on Shem and Japheth—before Noah’s long life closes.
text: Genesis 9:18–29 Genesis Noah’s three sons go forth from the ark to people the earth; then the rescued patriarch plants a vineyard, falls in shameful drunkenness, and a family crisis ends in curse on Canaan and blessing on Shem and Japheth—before Noah’s long life closes. The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.) Genesis 9:18 These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed. Genesis 9:19 Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. Genesis 9:20 He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. Genesis 9:21 And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside. Genesis 9:22 Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness. Genesis 9:23 When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him, Genesis 9:24 he said, “Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.” Genesis 9:25 He also said, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. Genesis 9:26 May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant.” Genesis 9:27 After the flood Noah lived 350 years. Genesis 9:28 All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died. Genesis 9:29

title: Isaiah 1:1–9
context: Isaiah son of Amoz sees concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Heaven and earth are summoned: the Lord has reared children who rebel. Ox and donkey know; Israel does not. A sinful nation is struck from head to foot. Country and cities lie desolate before foreigners. Zion is left like a booth. If the Lord of hosts had not left a few survivors, they would have been Sodom.
text: Isaiah 1:1–9 Isaiah Isaiah son of Amoz sees concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Heaven and earth are summoned: the Lord has reared children who rebel. Ox and donkey know; Israel does not. A sinful nation is struck from head to foot. Country and cities lie desolate before foreigners. Zion is left like a booth. If the Lord of hosts had not left a few survivors, they would have been Sodom. The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Isaiah 1:1 Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the Lord has spoken: “Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me. Isaiah 1:2 The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand.” Isaiah 1:3 Ah, sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, offspring of evildoers, children who deal corruptly! They have forsaken the Lord, they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged. Isaiah 1:4 Why will you still be struck down? Why will you continue to rebel? The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint. Isaiah 1:5 From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no soundness in it, but bruises and sores and raw wounds; they are not pressed out or bound up or softened with oil. Isaiah 1:6 Your country lies desolate, your cities are burned with fire; in your very presence foreigners devour your land; it is desolate, as overthrown by foreigners. Isaiah 1:7 And the daughter of Zion is left like a booth in a vineyard, like a lodge in a cucumber field, like a besieged city. Isaiah 1:8 If the Lord of hosts had not left us a few survivors, we should have been like Sodom, and become like Gomorrah. Isaiah 1:9

title: Isaiah 1:10–20
context: The remnant of 1:9 does not cancel the charge. Rulers of Judah are named Sodom, the people Gomorrah: hear the word. Multitudes of sacrifice, new moons, and spread hands cannot cover blood. Wash; cease evil; learn good; seek justice for fatherless and widow. Come, let us reason: scarlet may be snow. If willing and obedient, eat the good of the land; if they refuse, the sword—for the mouth of the Lord has spoken.
text: Isaiah 1:10–20 Isaiah The remnant of 1:9 does not cancel the charge. Rulers of Judah are named Sodom, the people Gomorrah: hear the word. Multitudes of sacrifice, new moons, and spread hands cannot cover blood. Wash; cease evil; learn good; seek justice for fatherless and widow. Come, let us reason: scarlet may be snow. If willing and obedient, eat the good of the land; if they refuse, the sword—for the mouth of the Lord has spoken. Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah! Isaiah 1:10 “What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord; I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed beasts; I do not delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of goats. Isaiah 1:11 When you come to appear before me, who has required of you this trampling of my courts? Isaiah 1:12 Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me. New moon and Sabbath and the calling of convocations—I cannot endure iniquity and solemn assembly. Isaiah 1:13 Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates; they have become a burden to me; I am weary of bearing them. Isaiah 1:14 When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood. Isaiah 1:15 Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes; cease to do evil, Isaiah 1:16 learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause. Isaiah 1:17 “Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool. Isaiah 1:18 If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; Isaiah 1:19 but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken.” Isaiah 1:20

title: Isaiah 1:21–31
context: After the offer of snow, the charge turns to the city: faithful Jerusalem has become a whore; silver is dross; princes love bribes and ignore widow and fatherless. The Mighty One of Israel will get relief from foes, smelt dross, restore judges, and name her righteous again. Zion is redeemed by justice; those who repent, by righteousness. Rebels are broken. Oaks and gardens of idolatry wither; the strong and his work burn, with none to quench.
text: Isaiah 1:21–31 Isaiah After the offer of snow, the charge turns to the city: faithful Jerusalem has become a whore; silver is dross; princes love bribes and ignore widow and fatherless. The Mighty One of Israel will get relief from foes, smelt dross, restore judges, and name her righteous again. Zion is redeemed by justice; those who repent, by righteousness. Rebels are broken. Oaks and gardens of idolatry wither; the strong and his work burn, with none to quench. How the faithful city has become a whore, she who was full of justice! Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers. Isaiah 1:21 Your silver has become dross, your best wine mixed with water. Isaiah 1:22 Your princes are rebels and companions of thieves. Everyone loves a bribe and runs after gifts. They do not bring justice to the fatherless, and the widow's cause does not come to them. Isaiah 1:23 Therefore the Lord declares, the Lord of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel: “Ah, I will get relief from my enemies and avenge myself on my foes. Isaiah 1:24 I will turn my hand against you and will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy. Isaiah 1:25 And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city.” Isaiah 1:26 Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness. Isaiah 1:27 But rebels and sinners shall be broken together, and those who forsake the Lord shall be consumed. Isaiah 1:28 For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired, and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen. Isaiah 1:29 For you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water. Isaiah 1:30 And the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark; both of them shall burn together, with none to quench them. Isaiah 1:31

title: Isaiah 10:1–4
context: Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and writers who keep writing oppression: they turn the needy from justice, rob the poor of their right, make widows spoil and the fatherless prey. What will you do on the day of punishment, the ruin from afar? To whom will you flee, and where leave your wealth? Nothing remains but to crouch among prisoners or fall among the slain. His anger has not turned away; his hand is stretched out still.
text: Isaiah 10:1–4 Isaiah Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and writers who keep writing oppression: they turn the needy from justice, rob the poor of their right, make widows spoil and the fatherless prey. What will you do on the day of punishment, the ruin from afar? To whom will you flee, and where leave your wealth? Nothing remains but to crouch among prisoners or fall among the slain. His anger has not turned away; his hand is stretched out still. Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression, Isaiah 10:1 to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right, that widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey! Isaiah 10:2 What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth? Isaiah 10:3 Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners or fall among the slain. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. Isaiah 10:4

title: Isaiah 10:20–34
context: In that day the remnant of Israel, survivors of Jacob, will no more lean on him who struck them, but on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. A remnant will return to the mighty God. Though Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant returns. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness. Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian: a little while, then the whip as at Midian and Egypt. The yoke broken because of the fat. He comes Aiath to Nob, shakes his fist at Zion—then the Lord lops the boughs; Lebanon falls by the Majestic One.
text: Isaiah 10:20–34 Isaiah In that day the remnant of Israel, survivors of Jacob, will no more lean on him who struck them, but on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. A remnant will return to the mighty God. Though Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant returns. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness. Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian: a little while, then the whip as at Midian and Egypt. The yoke broken because of the fat. He comes Aiath to Nob, shakes his fist at Zion—then the Lord lops the boughs; Lebanon falls by the Majestic One. In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. Isaiah 10:20 A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. Isaiah 10:21 For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness. Isaiah 10:22 For the Lord God of hosts will make a full end, as decreed, in the midst of all the earth. Isaiah 10:23 Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts: “O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian when he strikes you with his rod and lifts up his staff against you as the Egyptians did. Isaiah 10:24 For in a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction. Isaiah 10:25 And the Lord of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. And his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt. Isaiah 10:26 And in that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke will be broken because of the fat.” Isaiah 10:27 He has come to Aiath; he has passed through Migron; at Michmash he stores his baggage; Isaiah 10:28 they have crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodge for the night; Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul has fled. Isaiah 10:29 Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth! Isaiah 10:30 Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety. Isaiah 10:31 This very day he will halt at Nob; he will shake his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:32 Behold, the Lord God of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low. Isaiah 10:33 He will clear the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One. Isaiah 10:34

title: Isaiah 10:5–19
context: Ah, Assyria, the rod of the Lord’s anger; the staff in their hands is His fury. He sends him against a godless nation, to spoil and tread them like mire. But Assyria does not so intend: his heart is to destroy nations. He boasts his commanders are kings; Calno, Hamath, Samaria like the rest; he will do to Jerusalem’s idols as to Samaria’s. When the Lord has finished His work on Zion, He punishes the arrogant heart. The axe must not boast over the hewer. Therefore wasting and fire: the light of Israel becomes a flame; the forest’s remnant so few a child can write them.
text: Isaiah 10:5–19 Isaiah Ah, Assyria, the rod of the Lord’s anger; the staff in their hands is His fury. He sends him against a godless nation, to spoil and tread them like mire. But Assyria does not so intend: his heart is to destroy nations. He boasts his commanders are kings; Calno, Hamath, Samaria like the rest; he will do to Jerusalem’s idols as to Samaria’s. When the Lord has finished His work on Zion, He punishes the arrogant heart. The axe must not boast over the hewer. Therefore wasting and fire: the light of Israel becomes a flame; the forest’s remnant so few a child can write them. Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Isaiah 10:5 Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. Isaiah 10:6 But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few; Isaiah 10:7 for he says: “Are not my commanders all kings? Isaiah 10:8 Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus? Isaiah 10:9 As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria, Isaiah 10:10 shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?” Isaiah 10:11 When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes. Isaiah 10:12 For he says: “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding; I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures; like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones. Isaiah 10:13 My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples; and as one gathers eggs that have been left, so I have gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved a wing or opened its mouth or chirped.” Isaiah 10:14 Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? As if a rod should wield him who lifts it, or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood! Isaiah 10:15 Therefore the Lord God of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire. Isaiah 10:16 The light of Israel will become a fire, and his Holy One a flame, and it will burn and devour his thorns and briers in one day. Isaiah 10:17 The glory of his forest and of his fruitful land the Lord will destroy, both soul and body, and it will be as when a sick man wastes away. Isaiah 10:18 The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down. Isaiah 10:19

title: Isaiah 11:1–9
context: A shoot comes from the stump of Jesse; a branch from his roots bears fruit. The Spirit of the Lord rests on him: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear of the Lord. His delight is that fear. He does not judge by eyes or ears, but in righteousness for the poor and meek. He strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth; the breath of his lips kills the wicked. Righteousness and faithfulness are his belt. Wolf with lamb, leopard with goat, calf and lion together; a little child leads them. Cow and bear graze; the lion eats straw. The nursing child plays at the cobra’s hole. They shall not hurt in all my holy mountain: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord as waters cover the sea.
text: Isaiah 11:1–9 Isaiah A shoot comes from the stump of Jesse; a branch from his roots bears fruit. The Spirit of the Lord rests on him: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear of the Lord. His delight is that fear. He does not judge by eyes or ears, but in righteousness for the poor and meek. He strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth; the breath of his lips kills the wicked. Righteousness and faithfulness are his belt. Wolf with lamb, leopard with goat, calf and lion together; a little child leads them. Cow and bear graze; the lion eats straw. The nursing child plays at the cobra’s hole. They shall not hurt in all my holy mountain: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord as waters cover the sea. There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit. Isaiah 11:1 And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. Isaiah 11:2 And his delight shall be in the fear of the Lord. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, Isaiah 11:3 but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked. Isaiah 11:4 Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins. Isaiah 11:5 The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them. Isaiah 11:6 The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. Isaiah 11:7 The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. Isaiah 11:8 They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea. Isaiah 11:9

title: Isaiah 11:10–16
context: In that day the root of Jesse stands as a signal for the peoples; the nations inquire of him; his resting place is glorious. The Lord extends his hand a second time to recover the remnant from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the coastlands. He raises a signal, assembles the banished of Israel, gathers the dispersed of Judah from the four corners. Ephraim’s jealousy departs; they shall not harass one another. They swoop on Philistia and the east; Edom, Moab, Ammon. The Lord dries the Egyptian sea and the River into seven channels; a highway from Assyria for the remnant, as when Israel came up from Egypt.
text: Isaiah 11:10–16 Isaiah In that day the root of Jesse stands as a signal for the peoples; the nations inquire of him; his resting place is glorious. The Lord extends his hand a second time to recover the remnant from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the coastlands. He raises a signal, assembles the banished of Israel, gathers the dispersed of Judah from the four corners. Ephraim’s jealousy departs; they shall not harass one another. They swoop on Philistia and the east; Edom, Moab, Ammon. The Lord dries the Egyptian sea and the River into seven channels; a highway from Assyria for the remnant, as when Israel came up from Egypt. In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples—of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious. Isaiah 11:10 In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea. Isaiah 11:11 He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. Isaiah 11:12 The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim. Isaiah 11:13 But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them. Isaiah 11:14 And the Lord will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals. Isaiah 11:15 And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt. Isaiah 11:16

title: Isaiah 12:1–6
context: You will say in that day: I will give thanks, O Lord; though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. The Lord God is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. In that day: give thanks, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples. Sing, for he has done gloriously; let this be known in all the earth. Shout, inhabitant of Zion: great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.
text: Isaiah 12:1–6 Isaiah You will say in that day: I will give thanks, O Lord; though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. The Lord God is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. In that day: give thanks, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples. Sing, for he has done gloriously; let this be known in all the earth. Shout, inhabitant of Zion: great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel. You will say in that day: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. Isaiah 12:1 “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the Lord God is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.” Isaiah 12:2 With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. Isaiah 12:3 And you will say in that day: “Give thanks to the Lord, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted. Isaiah 12:4 “Sing praises to the Lord, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth. Isaiah 12:5 Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.” Isaiah 12:6

title: Isaiah 13:1–16
context: Isaiah the son of Amoz sees the oracle concerning Babylon: a signal on a bare hill, the LORD of hosts mustering a host from a distant land, the day of the LORD near as destruction from the Almighty. Hands go feeble and hearts melt; the land is made a desolation and its sinners destroyed from it. Sun, moon, and stars go dark in the overthrow of proud Babylon; people become rarer than gold; fugitives flee like a hunted gazelle; the sword and the atrocities of ancient siege fall on the city.
text: Isaiah 13:1–16 Isaiah Isaiah the son of Amoz sees the oracle concerning Babylon: a signal on a bare hill, the LORD of hosts mustering a host from a distant land, the day of the LORD near as destruction from the Almighty. Hands go feeble and hearts melt; the land is made a desolation and its sinners destroyed from it. Sun, moon, and stars go dark in the overthrow of proud Babylon; people become rarer than gold; fugitives flee like a hunted gazelle; the sword and the atrocities of ancient siege fall on the city. The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. Isaiah 13:1 On a bare hill raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. Isaiah 13:2 I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones. Isaiah 13:3 The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle. Isaiah 13:4 They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land. Isaiah 13:5 Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! Isaiah 13:6 Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. Isaiah 13:7 They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame. Isaiah 13:8 Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. Isaiah 13:9 For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light. Isaiah 13:10 I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless. Isaiah 13:11 I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir. Isaiah 13:12 Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger. Isaiah 13:13 And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. Isaiah 13:14 Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword. Isaiah 13:15 Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished. Isaiah 13:16

title: Isaiah 13:17–22
context: The LORD stirs up the Medes against Babylon: they have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold; their bows slaughter the young men, and they have no mercy on the fruit of the womb. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms and the pomp of the Chaldeans, falls like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them; the site is never inhabited, tents and shepherds gone, wild animals and howling creatures in the houses, ostriches and wild goats, hyenas in the towers and jackals in the palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.
text: Isaiah 13:17–22 Isaiah The LORD stirs up the Medes against Babylon: they have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold; their bows slaughter the young men, and they have no mercy on the fruit of the womb. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms and the pomp of the Chaldeans, falls like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them; the site is never inhabited, tents and shepherds gone, wild animals and howling creatures in the houses, ostriches and wild goats, hyenas in the towers and jackals in the palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged. Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold. Isaiah 13:17 Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children. Isaiah 13:18 And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. Isaiah 13:19 It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there. Isaiah 13:20 But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. Isaiah 13:21 Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged. Isaiah 13:22

title: Isaiah 14:1–11
context: The LORD has compassion on Jacob and again chooses Israel, setting them in their own land; sojourners join them, and they possess their former captors in the LORD’s land. After rest from pain, turmoil, and hard service they take up a taunt against the king of Babylon: the oppressor has ceased, the staff of the wicked is broken; the earth is quiet and the cedars of Lebanon rejoice; Sheol stirs the shades of dead kings to greet him, and his pomp is brought down to maggots and worms.
text: Isaiah 14:1–11 Isaiah The LORD has compassion on Jacob and again chooses Israel, setting them in their own land; sojourners join them, and they possess their former captors in the LORD’s land. After rest from pain, turmoil, and hard service they take up a taunt against the king of Babylon: the oppressor has ceased, the staff of the wicked is broken; the earth is quiet and the cedars of Lebanon rejoice; Sheol stirs the shades of dead kings to greet him, and his pomp is brought down to maggots and worms. For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land, and sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob. Isaiah 14:1 And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will possess them in the LORD’s land as male and female slaves. They will take captive those who were their captors, and rule over those who oppressed them. Isaiah 14:2 When the LORD has given you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve, Isaiah 14:3 you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased!” Isaiah 14:4 The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of rulers, Isaiah 14:5 that struck the peoples in wrath with unceasing blows, that ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution. Isaiah 14:6 The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing. Isaiah 14:7 The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, “Since you were laid low, no woodcutter comes up against us.” Isaiah 14:8 Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations. Isaiah 14:9 All of them will answer and say to you: “You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!” Isaiah 14:10 Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers. Isaiah 14:11

title: Isaiah 14:12–23
context: The taunt against the king of Babylon continues: the Day Star, son of Dawn, is fallen from heaven and cut down to the ground; he said in his heart he would ascend and make himself like the Most High, but he is brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit. Those who see him stare and ponder: is this the man who made the earth tremble? Kings of the nations lie in their tombs; he is cast out like a loathed branch, denied burial for destroying his land and slaying his people. The LORD of hosts cuts off from Babylon name and remnant and sweeps it with the broom of destruction.
text: Isaiah 14:12–23 Isaiah The taunt against the king of Babylon continues: the Day Star, son of Dawn, is fallen from heaven and cut down to the ground; he said in his heart he would ascend and make himself like the Most High, but he is brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit. Those who see him stare and ponder: is this the man who made the earth tremble? Kings of the nations lie in their tombs; he is cast out like a loathed branch, denied burial for destroying his land and slaying his people. The LORD of hosts cuts off from Babylon name and remnant and sweeps it with the broom of destruction. How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low! Isaiah 14:12 You said in your heart, “I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; Isaiah 14:13 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.” Isaiah 14:14 But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit. Isaiah 14:15 Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you: “Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, Isaiah 14:16 who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?” Isaiah 14:17 All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb; Isaiah 14:18 but you are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch, clothed with the slain, those pierced by the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit, like a dead body trampled underfoot. Isaiah 14:19 You will not be joined with them in burial, because you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. May the offspring of evildoers nevermore be named! Isaiah 14:20 Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers, lest they rise and possess the earth, and fill the face of the world with cities. Isaiah 14:21 “I will rise up against them,” declares the LORD of hosts, “and will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, descendants and posterity,” declares the LORD. Isaiah 14:22 “And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water, and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction,” declares the LORD of hosts. Isaiah 14:23

title: Isaiah 14:24–27
context: The LORD of hosts has sworn: as he has planned, so shall it be, and as he has purposed, so shall it stand. He will break the Assyrian in his land and on his mountains trample him underfoot; the yoke shall depart from them, and the burden from their shoulder. This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations. The LORD of hosts has purposed: who will annul it? His hand is stretched out: who will turn it back?

Isaiah 14:26 For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? Isaiah 14:27

title: Isaiah 14:28–32
context: In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle: rejoice not, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken, for from the serpent’s root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent. The firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy lie down in safety; but I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant it will slay. Wail, O gate; cry out, O city; melt in fear, O Philistia, all of you! For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks. What will one answer the messengers of the nation? The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge.

title: Isaiah 15:1–9
context: An oracle concerning Moab: Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, and Moab is undone; Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, and Moab is undone. He has gone up to the temple and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn. In the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears. Heshbon and Elealeh cry out as far as Jahaz; the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. A heart cries out for Moab; fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah, weeping on the ascent of Luhith and raising a cry of destruction on the road to Horonaim. The waters of Nimrim are a desolation; they carry what they have laid up over the Brook of the Willows. A cry goes around the land of Moab; the waters of Dibon are full of blood, and a lion waits for those who escape, for the remnant of the land.

Isaiah 15:1 He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn. Isaiah 15:2 in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears. Isaiah 15:3 Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. Isaiah 15:4 My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction. Isaiah 15:5 the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more. Isaiah 15:6 Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows. Isaiah 15:7 For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim. Isaiah 15:8 For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land. Isaiah 15:9

title: Isaiah 16:1–14
context: Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion. Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon. Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land, then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness. We have heard of the pride of Moab—how proud he is!—of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right. Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth. For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea. Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased. And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting. Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth. And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail. This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. But now the LORD has spoken, saying, In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble.

title: Isaiah 17:1–14
context: An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. The cities of Aroer deserted for flocks; the fortress gone from Ephraim and the kingdom from Damascus; the glory of Jacob brought low, gleanings like an olive tree beaten. In that day man will look to his Maker, not to altars his fingers made. Pleasant plants and a stranger’s vine-branch, then a harvest that flees in grief. Ah, the thunder of many peoples; he rebukes them, and at evening terror, before morning they are no more. The unit stays with historic Damascus and Ephraim in the Assyria age—Syria’s league with the northern kingdom against Judah, Tiglath-pileser’s stroke—as Wesley and Calvin actually read—not a newspaper of later states, not a millennial camp fight.

Isaiah 17:1 The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid. Isaiah 17:2 The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts. Isaiah 17:3 And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean. Isaiah 17:4 And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. Isaiah 17:5 Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten—two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel. Isaiah 17:6 In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah 17:7 He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense. Isaiah 17:8 In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. Isaiah 17:9 For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger, Isaiah 17:10 though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain. Isaiah 17:11 Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! Isaiah 17:12 The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. Isaiah 17:13 At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us. Isaiah 17:14

title: Isaiah 18:1–7
context: Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, which sends ambassadors by the sea in vessels of papyrus. Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, feared near and far, whose land the rivers divide. All inhabitants of the world, when a signal is raised, look; when a trumpet is blown, hear. The LORD quietly looks from his dwelling like clear heat and a cloud of dew in harvest; before the harvest he cuts off the shoots. Birds of prey summer on them, beasts winter on them. At that time tribute is brought to the LORD of hosts from that people to Mount Zion. The unit stays with historic Cush beyond the rivers of Ethiopia in the Assyria age—ambassadors, papyrus boats, a present to Zion—as Wesley and Calvin actually read—not a newspaper of later states, not a millennial camp fight.

Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. Isaiah 18:2 All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear! Isaiah 18:3 For thus the LORD said to me: “I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” Isaiah 18:4 For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. Isaiah 18:5 They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. Isaiah 18:6 At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts. Isaiah 18:7

title: Isaiah 19:1–15
context: An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; the idols tremble, hearts melt. Egyptians against Egyptians, city against city; the spirit emptied, counsel confounded; they inquire of idols and necromancers. A hard master, a fierce king. Waters of the sea dried, the Nile parched, canals foul, reeds rot, sown ground gone; fishermen mourn, flax-workers despair, pillars crushed. Princes of Zoan foolish, princes of Memphis deluded; the LORD mingles a spirit of confusion; nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do. Isaiah 19:1 And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; Isaiah 19:2 and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers; Isaiah 19:3 and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the LORD God of hosts. Isaiah 19:4 And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched, Isaiah 19:5 and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. Isaiah 19:6 There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more. Isaiah 19:7 The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. Isaiah 19:8 The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. Isaiah 19:9 Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved. Isaiah 19:10 The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”? Isaiah 19:12 The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger. Isaiah 19:13 The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit. Isaiah 2:6 Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures; their land is filled with horses, and there is no end to their chariots. Isaiah 2:7 Their land is filled with idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their own fingers have made. Isaiah 2:8 So man is humbled, and each one is brought low—do not forgive them! Isaiah 2:9 Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the Lord, and from the splendor of his majesty. Isaiah 2:10 The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. Isaiah 2:11 For the Lord of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up—and it shall be brought low; Isaiah 2:12 against all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up; and against all the oaks of Bashan; Isaiah 2:13 against all the lofty mountains, and against all the uplifted hills; Isaiah 2:14 against every high tower, and against every fortified wall; Isaiah 2:15 against all the ships of Tarshish, and against all the beautiful craft. Isaiah 2:16 And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. Isaiah 2:17 And the idols shall utterly pass away. Isaiah 2:18 And people shall enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground, from before the terror of the Lord, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. Isaiah 2:19 In that day mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats, Isaiah 2:20 to enter the caverns of the rocks and the clefts of the cliffs, from before the terror of the Lord, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth. Isaiah 2:21 Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he? Isaiah 2:22

Isaiah 28:1 Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest, like a storm of mighty, overflowing waters, he casts down to the earth with his hand. Isaiah 28:2 The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot; Isaiah 28:3 and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand. Isaiah 28:4 In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people, Isaiah 28:5 and a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate. Isaiah 28:6 These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed by wine, they stagger with strong drink, they reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment. Isaiah 28:9 For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little.” Isaiah 28:10 For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people, Isaiah 28:11 to whom he has said, “This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose”; yet they would not hear. Isaiah 28:12 And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little, that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.
