Still the canonical ESV text is to be read pastorally: at dawn Jesus teaches in the temple; scribes and Pharisees thrust a woman caught in adultery into the midst to trap him between Moses’ sentence and his mercy; he writes on the ground, sends the sinless-first stone, and tells her, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. John 8:1 Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them. John 8:2 The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst John 8:3 they said to him, “Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery. John 8:4 Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?” John 8:5 This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground. John 8:6 And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” John 8:7 And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground. John 8:8 But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. John 8:9 Jesus stood up and said to her, “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” John 8:10 She said, “No one, Lord.” And Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” John 8:11

title: John 8:12–20
context: After the bracketed pericope, the ESV resumes the temple discourse of Tabernacles. Jesus names himself the light of the world and promises that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness. Pharisees object that self-witness is invalid. He answers with origin and destiny, refuses flesh-judgment, and claims the two-witness rule of their Law: he and the Father who sent him. They ask where his Father is; he says they know neither him nor the Father. He speaks these words in the treasury; no one arrests him, because his hour has not yet come.
text: John 8:12–20 John After the bracketed pericope, the ESV resumes the temple discourse of Tabernacles. Jesus names himself the light of the world and promises that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness. Pharisees object that self-witness is invalid. He answers with origin and destiny, refuses flesh-judgment, and claims the two-witness rule of their Law: he and the Father who sent him. They ask where his Father is; he says they know neither him nor the Father. He speaks these words in the treasury; no one arrests him, because his hour has not yet come. Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” John 8:12 So the Pharisees said to him, “You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true.” John 8:13 Jesus answered, “Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going. John 8:14 You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. John 8:15 Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me. John 8:16 In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. John 8:17 I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me.” John 8:18 They said to him therefore, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” John 8:19 These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come. John 8:20

title: John 8:21–30
context: Still in the temple, Jesus says he is going away; they will seek him and die in their sin; where he goes they cannot come. They joke about suicide. He contrasts below and above, this world and not of this world, and warns that unless they believe that “I am he” they will die in their sins. They ask who he is. He speaks of the true Sender and of being lifted up as Son of Man—then they will know that I am he. The Father has not left him alone, for he always does what pleases him. As he says these things, many believed in him.
text: John 8:21–30 John Still in the temple, Jesus says he is going away; they will seek him and die in their sin; where he goes they cannot come. They joke about suicide. He contrasts below and above, this world and not of this world, and warns that unless they believe that “I am he” they will die in their sins. They ask who he is. He speaks of the true Sender and of being lifted up as Son of Man—then they will know that I am he. The Father has not left him alone, for he always does what pleases him. As he says these things, many believed in him. So he said to them again, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” John 8:21 So the Jews said, “Will he kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?” John 8:22 He said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. John 8:23 I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins.” John 8:24 So they said to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. John 8:25 I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him.” John 8:26 They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. John 8:27 So Jesus said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me. John 8:28 And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” John 8:29 As he was saying these things, many believed in him. John 8:30

title: John 8:31–47
context: Jesus turns to Jews who had believed him: if you abide in my word you are truly disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. They protest Abrahamic freedom. He answers that everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin; the slave does not remain in the house forever, the son does; if the Son sets you free, you are free indeed. Offspring of Abraham still seek to kill him because his word finds no place in them. Abraham’s children would do Abraham’s works; instead they do their father’s. They claim God as Father; he says if God were their Father they would love him. They cannot bear to hear his word because they are of their father the devil, a murderer and liar. Whoever is of God hears God’s words; the reason they do not hear is that they are not of God.
text: John 8:31–47 John Jesus turns to Jews who had believed him: if you abide in my word you are truly disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. They protest Abrahamic freedom. He answers that everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin; the slave does not remain in the house forever, the son does; if the Son sets you free, you are free indeed. Offspring of Abraham still seek to kill him because his word finds no place in them. Abraham’s children would do Abraham’s works; instead they do their father’s. They claim God as Father; he says if God were their Father they would love him. They cannot bear to hear his word because they are of their father the devil, a murderer and liar. Whoever is of God hears God’s words; the reason they do not hear is that they are not of God. So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, John 8:31 and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” John 8:32 They answered him, “We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, ‘You will become free’?” John 8:33 Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin. John 8:34 The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. John 8:35 So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed. John 8:36 I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. John 8:37 I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father.” John 8:38 They answered him, “Abraham is our father.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, John 8:39 but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did. John 8:40 You are doing the works your father did.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father—even God.” John 8:41 Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me. John 8:42 Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. John 8:43 You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies. John 8:44 But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. John 8:45 Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? John 8:46 Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God.” John 8:47

title: John 8:48–59
context: The dispute turns to insult and then to glory. They call Jesus a Samaritan and say he has a demon. He denies the demon, honors the Father, and does not seek his own glory. If anyone keeps his word, he will never see death. They hear bodily immortality, invoke Abraham and the prophets who died, and ask who he makes himself. He answers that the Father glorifies him; they have not known God; Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They scoff that he is not yet fifty. He answers with the divine present: before Abraham was, I am. They pick up stones; he hides himself and goes out of the temple.
text: John 8:48–59 John The dispute turns to insult and then to glory. They call Jesus a Samaritan and say he has a demon. He denies the demon, honors the Father, and does not seek his own glory. If anyone keeps his word, he will never see death. They hear bodily immortality, invoke Abraham and the prophets who died, and ask who he makes himself. He answers that the Father glorifies him; they have not known God; Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They scoff that he is not yet fifty. He answers with the divine present: before Abraham was, I am. They pick up stones; he hides himself and goes out of the temple. The Jews answered him, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” John 8:48 Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. John 8:49 Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge. John 8:50 Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.” John 8:51 The Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.’ John 8:52 Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?” John 8:53 Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ‘He is our God.’ John 8:54 But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word. John 8:55 Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad.” John 8:56 So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” John 8:57 Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.” John 8:58 So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple. John 8:59

title: John 9:1–12
context: As he passes by, Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask who sinned. Jesus refuses the dilemma: it was not that this man or his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. Night is coming; while he is in the world he is the light. He makes mud with spit, anoints the man’s eyes, and sends him to Siloam (Sent). The man goes, washes, and comes seeing. Neighbors dispute his identity; he testifies that he is the man, and that he does not know where Jesus is.
text: John 9:1–12 John As he passes by, Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask who sinned. Jesus refuses the dilemma: it was not that this man or his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. Night is coming; while he is in the world he is the light. He makes mud with spit, anoints the man’s eyes, and sends him to Siloam (Sent). The man goes, washes, and comes seeing. Neighbors dispute his identity; he testifies that he is the man, and that he does not know where Jesus is. As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. John 9:1 And his disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” John 9:2 Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. John 9:3 We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work. John 9:4 As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” John 9:5 Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man’s eyes with the mud John 9:6 and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing. John 9:7 The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?” John 9:8 Some said, “It is he.” Others said, “No, but he is like him.” He kept saying, “I am the man.” John 9:9 So they said to him, “Then how were your eyes opened?” John 9:10 He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed and received my sight.” John 9:11 They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I do not know.” John 9:12

title: John 9:13–34
context: Neighbors bring the healed man to the Pharisees. It was Sabbath when Jesus made the mud. Division follows: this man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath—or how can a sinner do such signs? The man says he is a prophet. Leaders will not believe he had been blind until they grill the parents, who fear synagogue-expulsion and defer: he is of age. A second interrogation demands, Give glory to God; we know this man is a sinner. One thing I know: I was blind, now I see. They revile him; he reasons from the unprecedented sign; they say he was born in utter sin and cast him out.
text: John 9:13–34 John Neighbors bring the healed man to the Pharisees. It was Sabbath when Jesus made the mud. Division follows: this man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath—or how can a sinner do such signs? The man says he is a prophet. Leaders will not believe he had been blind until they grill the parents, who fear synagogue-expulsion and defer: he is of age. A second interrogation demands, Give glory to God; we know this man is a sinner. One thing I know: I was blind, now I see. They revile him; he reasons from the unprecedented sign; they say he was born in utter sin and cast him out. They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind. John 9:13 Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. John 9:14 So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.” John 9:15 Some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” And there was a division among them. John 9:16 So they said again to the blind man, “What do you say about him, since he has opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.” John 9:17 The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight John 9:18 and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” John 9:19 His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. John 9:20 But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.” John 9:21 (His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he was to be put out of the synagogue. John 9:22 Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”) John 9:23 So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” John 9:24 He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.” John 9:25 They said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” John 9:26 He answered them, “I have told you already, and you would not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?” John 9:27 And they reviled him, saying, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. John 9:28 We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.” John 9:29 The man answered, “Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. John 9:30 We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him. John 9:31 Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. John 9:32 If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” John 9:33 They answered him, “You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?” And they cast him out. John 9:34

title: John 9:35–41
context: Jesus hears that they have cast him out, finds him, and asks, Do you believe in the Son of Man? The man asks who he is, that he may believe; Jesus answers, you have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you. Lord, I believe—and he worships. Jesus: for judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Some Pharisees ask, Are we also blind? If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, We see, your guilt remains.
text: John 9:35–41 John Jesus hears that they have cast him out, finds him, and asks, Do you believe in the Son of Man? The man asks who he is, that he may believe; Jesus answers, you have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you. Lord, I believe—and he worships. Jesus: for judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Some Pharisees ask, Are we also blind? If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, We see, your guilt remains. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” John 9:35 He answered, “And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?” John 9:36 Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you.” John 9:37 He said, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped him. John 9:38 Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” John 9:39 Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” John 9:40 Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, ‘We see,’ your guilt remains.” John 9:41

title: Matthew 1:1–17
context: Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ—tracing the Messiah from Abraham and David through exile to Joseph and Mary—so that readers see promise fulfilled and a Savior who belongs to Israel’s story.
text: Matthew 1:1–17 Matthew Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ—tracing the Messiah from Abraham and David through exile to Joseph and Mary—so that readers see promise fulfilled and a Savior who belongs to Israel’s story. The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Matthew 1:1 Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, Matthew 1:2 and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, Matthew 1:3 and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, Matthew 1:4 and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, Matthew 1:5 and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, Matthew 1:6 and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, Matthew 1:7 and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, Matthew 1:8 and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, Matthew 1:9 and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, Matthew 1:10 and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. Matthew 1:11 And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, Matthew 1:12 and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, Matthew 1:13 and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, Matthew 1:14 and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, Matthew 1:15 and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. Matthew 1:16 So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. Matthew 1:17

title: Matthew 1:18–25
context: After the genealogy, Matthew narrates Jesus’ birth: Mary’s virginal conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s righteous struggle and obedience, the naming of Jesus as Savior, and the fulfillment of Isaiah’s Immanuel promise.
text: Matthew 1:18–25 Matthew After the genealogy, Matthew narrates Jesus’ birth: Mary’s virginal conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s righteous struggle and obedience, the naming of Jesus as Savior, and the fulfillment of Isaiah’s Immanuel promise. Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Matthew 1:18 And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. Matthew 1:19 But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. Matthew 1:20 She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” Matthew 1:21 All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: Matthew 1:22 “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). Matthew 1:23 When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, Matthew 1:24 but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus. Matthew 1:25

title: Matthew 10:1–4
context: After mercy and conflict in Galilee, Jesus calls the Twelve, gives them authority over spirits and sickness, and names them as apostles. The mission discourse begins with a named circle—ordinary men under the King’s delegated power, including the one who will betray Him.
text: Matthew 10:1–4 Matthew After mercy and conflict in Galilee, Jesus calls the Twelve, gives them authority over spirits and sickness, and names them as apostles. The mission discourse begins with a named circle—ordinary men under the King’s delegated power, including the one who will betray Him. And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. Matthew 10:1 The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Matthew 10:2 Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Matthew 10:3 Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. Matthew 10:4

title: Matthew 10:16–23
context: Jesus widens the mission charge into realism: sheep among wolves, courts and kings, family betrayal, hatred for His name, endurance unto salvation, and flight from town to town until the Son of Man comes. Courage here is Spirit-supplied witness, not naïveté.
text: Matthew 10:16–23 Matthew Jesus widens the mission charge into realism: sheep among wolves, courts and kings, family betrayal, hatred for His name, endurance unto salvation, and flight from town to town until the Son of Man comes. Courage here is Spirit-supplied witness, not naïveté. “Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Matthew 10:16 Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues, Matthew 10:17 and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. Matthew 10:18 When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. Matthew 10:19 For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. Matthew 10:20 Brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death, Matthew 10:21 and you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. Matthew 10:22 When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly, I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Matthew 10:23

title: Matthew 10:24–33
context: Jesus reframes fear: disciples share the Master’s mistreatment, yet must proclaim openly. Fear God rather than body-killers; trust the Father who numbers hairs and values sparrows; acknowledge Christ before people, for He will acknowledge or deny before the Father.
text: Matthew 10:24–33 Matthew Jesus reframes fear: disciples share the Master’s mistreatment, yet must proclaim openly. Fear God rather than body-killers; trust the Father who numbers hairs and values sparrows; acknowledge Christ before people, for He will acknowledge or deny before the Father. “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. Matthew 10:24 It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they malign those of his household. Matthew 10:25 “So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. Matthew 10:26 What I tell you in the dark, say in the light, and what you hear whispered, proclaim on the housetops. Matthew 10:27 And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Matthew 10:28 Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. Matthew 10:29 But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Matthew 10:30 Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. Matthew 10:31 So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven, Matthew 10:32 but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 10:33

title: Matthew 10:34–39
context: Jesus corrects false expectations of easy peace: His coming divides households, demands supreme love, requires the cross, and inverts life’s calculus—finding life by losing it for His sake. Allegiance to the King outranks every natural bond.
text: Matthew 10:34–39 Matthew Jesus corrects false expectations of easy peace: His coming divides households, demands supreme love, requires the cross, and inverts life’s calculus—finding life by losing it for His sake. Allegiance to the King outranks every natural bond. “Do not think that I have come to bring peace to the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. Matthew 10:34 For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Matthew 10:35 And a person’s enemies will be those of his own household. Matthew 10:36 Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. Matthew 10:37 And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Matthew 10:38 Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Matthew 10:39

title: Matthew 10:40–42
context: The discourse closes with hospitality theology: receiving messengers is receiving Christ and the Father; prophetic and righteous welcome carry matching reward; even a cup of cold water to a little disciple is remembered. Mission hardship is matched by kingdom honor for those who welcome the sent.
text: Matthew 10:40–42 Matthew The discourse closes with hospitality theology: receiving messengers is receiving Christ and the Father; prophetic and righteous welcome carry matching reward; even a cup of cold water to a little disciple is remembered. Mission hardship is matched by kingdom honor for those who welcome the sent. “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Matthew 10:40 The one who receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and the one who receives a righteous person because he is a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. Matthew 10:41 And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water because he is a disciple, truly, I say to you, he will by no means lose his reward.” Matthew 10:42

title: Matthew 10:5–15
context: Jesus sends the Twelve on a time-bound mission to Israel’s lost sheep: proclaim the kingdom, heal freely, travel light, seek worthy houses, and treat rejection with solemn witness. Priority to Israel here does not cancel later Gentile mission; it honors covenant order as the King advances.
text: Matthew 10:5–15 Matthew Jesus sends the Twelve on a time-bound mission to Israel’s lost sheep: proclaim the kingdom, heal freely, travel light, seek worthy houses, and treat rejection with solemn witness. Priority to Israel here does not cancel later Gentile mission; it honors covenant order as the King advances. These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, Matthew 10:5 but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Matthew 10:6 And proclaim as you go, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’ Matthew 10:7 Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay. Matthew 10:8 Acquire no gold or silver or copper for your belts, Matthew 10:9 no bag for your journey, or two tunics or sandals or a staff, for the laborer deserves his food. Matthew 10:10 And whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it and stay there until you depart. Matthew 10:11 As you enter the house, greet it. Matthew 10:12 And if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it, but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you. Matthew 10:13 And if anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet when you leave that house or town. Matthew 10:14 Truly, I say to you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. Matthew 10:15

title: Matthew 11:1–6
context: After commissioning the Twelve (ch. 10), Jesus resumes His own ministry while John the Baptist—now in prison—sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with Isaiah-shaped messianic works and a beatitude for those not offended by Him.
text: Matthew 11:1–6 Matthew After commissioning the Twelve (ch. 10), Jesus resumes His own ministry while John the Baptist—now in prison—sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with Isaiah-shaped messianic works and a beatitude for those not offended by Him. When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. Matthew 11:1 Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples Matthew 11:2 and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” Matthew 11:3 And Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: Matthew 11:4 the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. Matthew 11:5 And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” Matthew 11:6

title: Matthew 11:16–19
context: After honoring John before the crowds (vv. 7–15), Jesus turns to diagnose “this generation”: like quarrelsome children in the marketplaces, it refuses both John’s austere call and the Son of Man’s table fellowship—yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.
text: Matthew 11:16–19 Matthew After honoring John before the crowds (vv. 7–15), Jesus turns to diagnose “this generation”: like quarrelsome children in the marketplaces, it refuses both John’s austere call and the Son of Man’s table fellowship—yet wisdom is justified by her deeds. “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates, Matthew 11:16 “‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ Matthew 11:17 For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ Matthew 11:18 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” Matthew 11:19

title: Matthew 11:20–24
context: After exposing this generation’s refusal of both John’s austerity and the Son of Man’s table fellowship (vv. 16–19), Jesus denounces the Galilean cities where most of His mighty works had been done—Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—comparing their unrepentance with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom.
text: Matthew 11:20–24 Matthew After exposing this generation’s refusal of both John’s austerity and the Son of Man’s table fellowship (vv. 16–19), Jesus denounces the Galilean cities where most of His mighty works had been done—Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—comparing their unrepentance with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom. Then he began to denounce the cities where most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent. Matthew 11:20 “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Matthew 11:21 But I tell you, it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. Matthew 11:22 And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Matthew 11:23 But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.” Matthew 11:24

title: Matthew 11:25–27
context: After pronouncing woes on unrepentant cities (vv. 20–24), Jesus turns from indictment to thanksgiving. He praises the Father—Lord of heaven and earth—for a revelatory will that hides kingdom truth from the self-wise and discloses it to “little children,” then speaks of the Son’s exclusive knowledge of the Father and of those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.
text: Matthew 11:25–27 Matthew After pronouncing woes on unrepentant cities (vv. 20–24), Jesus turns from indictment to thanksgiving. He praises the Father—Lord of heaven and earth—for a revelatory will that hides kingdom truth from the self-wise and discloses it to “little children,” then speaks of the Son’s exclusive knowledge of the Father and of those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. At that time Jesus declared, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; Matthew 11:25 yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. Matthew 11:26 All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” Matthew 11:27

title: Matthew 11:28–30
context: From thanksgiving over the Father’s revelatory will (vv. 25–27), Jesus turns outward to the weary. He invites all who labor and are heavy laden to come to Him for rest, to take His yoke, learn from His gentleness and lowliness, and find that His yoke is easy and His burden light.
text: Matthew 11:28–30 Matthew From thanksgiving over the Father’s revelatory will (vv. 25–27), Jesus turns outward to the weary. He invites all who labor and are heavy laden to come to Him for rest, to take His yoke, learn from His gentleness and lowliness, and find that His yoke is easy and His burden light. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Matthew 11:28 Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. Matthew 11:29 For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” Matthew 11:30

title: Matthew 11:7–15
context: After John’s disciples leave with Jesus’ answer (vv. 2–6), Jesus turns to the crowds and interprets John’s ministry: the Baptist is no reed or soft courtier but more than a prophet—Malachi’s messenger, Elijah who is to come—yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
text: Matthew 11:7–15 Matthew After John’s disciples leave with Jesus’ answer (vv. 2–6), Jesus turns to the crowds and interprets John’s ministry: the Baptist is no reed or soft courtier but more than a prophet—Malachi’s messenger, Elijah who is to come—yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? Matthew 11:7 What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings' houses. Matthew 11:8 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. Matthew 11:9 This is he of whom it is written, “‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ Matthew 11:10 Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. Matthew 11:11 From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. Matthew 11:12 For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, Matthew 11:13 and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. Matthew 11:14 He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Matthew 11:15

title: Matthew 12:1–8
context: Following Jesus’ invitation to the weary (11:28–30), Matthew narrates a Sabbath controversy: the disciples pluck grain, the Pharisees accuse, and Jesus answers from Scripture—David, the temple priests, Hosea’s “mercy,” and His own lordship of the Sabbath.
text: Matthew 12:1–8 Matthew Following Jesus’ invitation to the weary (11:28–30), Matthew narrates a Sabbath controversy: the disciples pluck grain, the Pharisees accuse, and Jesus answers from Scripture—David, the temple priests, Hosea’s “mercy,” and His own lordship of the Sabbath. At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. Matthew 12:1 But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” Matthew 12:2 He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: Matthew 12:3 how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? Matthew 12:4 Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? Matthew 12:5 I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. Matthew 12:6 And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. Matthew 12:7 For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” Matthew 12:8

title: Matthew 12:15–21
context: After the Pharisees conspire to destroy Him (12:14), Jesus withdraws; crowds follow and He heals them all, charging silence. Matthew reads the scene as Isaiah 42 fulfilled—the chosen Servant who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until He brings justice to victory, and in whose name the nations hope.
text: Matthew 12:15–21 Matthew After the Pharisees conspire to destroy Him (12:14), Jesus withdraws; crowds follow and He heals them all, charging silence. Matthew reads the scene as Isaiah 42 fulfilled—the chosen Servant who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until He brings justice to victory, and in whose name the nations hope. Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all Matthew 12:15 and ordered them not to make him known. Matthew 12:16 This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: Matthew 12:17 “Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. Matthew 12:18 He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; Matthew 12:19 a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory; Matthew 12:20 and in his name the Gentiles will hope.” Matthew 12:21

title: Matthew 12:22–32
context: After Sabbath controversy and Isaiah’s Servant song (12:1–21), Matthew narrates a Spirit-worked deliverance: Jesus heals a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute. Crowds wonder about the Son of David; Pharisees attribute the exorcism to Beelzebul. Jesus answers with kingdom logic, the strong man bound, and a solemn warning about blasphemy against the Spirit.
text: Matthew 12:22–32 Matthew After Sabbath controversy and Isaiah’s Servant song (12:1–21), Matthew narrates a Spirit-worked deliverance: Jesus heals a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute. Crowds wonder about the Son of David; Pharisees attribute the exorcism to Beelzebul. Jesus answers with kingdom logic, the strong man bound, and a solemn warning about blasphemy against the Spirit. Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. Matthew 12:22 And all the people were amazed, and said, “Can this be the Son of David?” Matthew 12:23 But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons.” Matthew 12:24 Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand. Matthew 12:25 And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? Matthew 12:26 And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. Matthew 12:27 But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Matthew 12:28 Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house. Matthew 12:29 Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Matthew 12:30 Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. Matthew 12:31 And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Matthew 12:32

title: Matthew 12:33–37
context: After the Beelzebul charge and the warning about blasphemy against the Spirit (12:22–32), Jesus presses the Pharisees with tree-and-fruit logic: speech flows from the heart’s treasure, and on judgment day careless words will justify or condemn.
text: Matthew 12:33–37 Matthew After the Beelzebul charge and the warning about blasphemy against the Spirit (12:22–32), Jesus presses the Pharisees with tree-and-fruit logic: speech flows from the heart’s treasure, and on judgment day careless words will justify or condemn. “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit. Matthew 12:33 You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Matthew 12:34 The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. Matthew 12:35 I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, Matthew 12:36 for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Matthew 12:37

title: Matthew 12:38–42
context: After tree-and-fruit warnings and the accounting of careless words (12:33–37), some scribes and Pharisees answer Jesus by asking for a sign. He refuses spectacle to unbelief, promises only the sign of Jonah—His own death and rising—and warns that Nineveh and the queen of the South will condemn this generation, for something greater than Jonah and Solomon is here.
text: Matthew 12:38–42 Matthew After tree-and-fruit warnings and the accounting of careless words (12:33–37), some scribes and Pharisees answer Jesus by asking for a sign. He refuses spectacle to unbelief, promises only the sign of Jonah—His own death and rising—and warns that Nineveh and the queen of the South will condemn this generation, for something greater than Jonah and Solomon is here. Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” Matthew 12:38 But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Matthew 12:39 For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Matthew 12:40 The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. Matthew 12:41 The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.” Matthew 12:42

title: Matthew 12:43–45
context: After the demand for a sign and Jesus’ reply from Jonah, Nineveh, and the queen of the South (12:38–42), He warns with a brief parable: an unclean spirit departs, returns to an empty house, and the last state is worse—applied to “this evil generation.”
text: Matthew 12:43–45 Matthew After the demand for a sign and Jesus’ reply from Jonah, Nineveh, and the queen of the South (12:38–42), He warns with a brief parable: an unclean spirit departs, returns to an empty house, and the last state is worse—applied to “this evil generation.” “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none. Matthew 12:43 Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Matthew 12:44 Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.” Matthew 12:45

title: Matthew 12:46–50
context: After the demand for a sign and the warning about the returning unclean spirit (12:38–45), Matthew closes the chapter with a family interruption: while Jesus is still speaking, His mother and brothers stand outside asking to speak with Him—and He redefines true kinship around discipleship and the Father’s will.
text: Matthew 12:46–50 Matthew After the demand for a sign and the warning about the returning unclean spirit (12:38–45), Matthew closes the chapter with a family interruption: while Jesus is still speaking, His mother and brothers stand outside asking to speak with Him—and He redefines true kinship around discipleship and the Father’s will. While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. Matthew 12:46 Someone told him, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you.” Matthew 12:47 But he replied to the man who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” Matthew 12:48 And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! Matthew 12:49 For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.” Matthew 12:50

title: Matthew 12:9–14
context: Continuing the Sabbath controversy (12:1–8), Jesus enters the synagogue, faces a trap question over a man with a withered hand, answers with mercy’s logic, heals, and draws the Pharisees into a plot to destroy Him.
text: Matthew 12:9–14 Matthew Continuing the Sabbath controversy (12:1–8), Jesus enters the synagogue, faces a trap question over a man with a withered hand, answers with mercy’s logic, heals, and draws the Pharisees into a plot to destroy Him. He went on from there and entered their synagogue. Matthew 12:9 And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”—so that they might accuse him. Matthew 12:10 He said to them, “Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Matthew 12:11 Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” Matthew 12:12 Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. Matthew 12:13 But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. Matthew 12:14

title: Matthew 13:1–9
context: On the same day as the conflicts of chapter 12, Jesus leaves the house, sits beside the sea, and teaches great crowds from a boat. Matthew opens a concentrated block of kingdom teaching in parables—beginning with the Sower—where hearing the word becomes the hinge of discipleship.
text: Matthew 13:1–9 Matthew On the same day as the conflicts of chapter 12, Jesus leaves the house, sits beside the sea, and teaches great crowds from a boat. Matthew opens a concentrated block of kingdom teaching in parables—beginning with the Sower—where hearing the word becomes the hinge of discipleship. That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. Matthew 13:1 And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach. Matthew 13:2 And he told them many things in parables, saying: “A sower went out to sow. Matthew 13:3 And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them. Matthew 13:4 Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, Matthew 13:5 but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away. Matthew 13:6 Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Matthew 13:7 Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. Matthew 13:8 He who has ears, let him hear.” Matthew 13:9

title: Matthew 13:10–17
context: After the Sower parable, the disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables. He answers with the gift of kingdom secrets, Isaiah’s judgment oracle on dull hearts, and a blessing on eyes and ears that truly see and hear—framing how the word divides hearers.
text: Matthew 13:10–17 Matthew After the Sower parable, the disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables. He answers with the gift of kingdom secrets, Isaiah’s judgment oracle on dull hearts, and a blessing on eyes and ears that truly see and hear—framing how the word divides hearers. Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” Matthew 13:10 And he answered them, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. Matthew 13:11 For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Matthew 13:12 This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. Matthew 13:13 Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: “‘“You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.” Matthew 13:14 For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ Matthew 13:15 But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. Matthew 13:16 For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. Matthew 13:17

title: Matthew 13:18–23
context: Jesus explains the Sower to the disciples: four soils picture four hearings of the kingdom word—snatched, shallow, choked, and fruitful. Understanding and endurance become the pastoral hinge of the parable’s meaning.
text: Matthew 13:18–23 Matthew Jesus explains the Sower to the disciples: four soils picture four hearings of the kingdom word—snatched, shallow, choked, and fruitful. Understanding and endurance become the pastoral hinge of the parable’s meaning. “Hear then the parable of the sower: Matthew 13:18 When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. Matthew 13:19 As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, Matthew 13:20 yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. Matthew 13:21 As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. Matthew 13:22 As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” Matthew 13:23

title: Matthew 13:24–30
context: Jesus sets another kingdom parable before the crowds: good seed sown in a field, an enemy’s weeds mixed among the wheat, and a master’s patience until harvest. Premature uprooting is refused; final separation is reserved for the reapers.
text: Matthew 13:24–30 Matthew Jesus sets another kingdom parable before the crowds: good seed sown in a field, an enemy’s weeds mixed among the wheat, and a master’s patience until harvest. Premature uprooting is refused; final separation is reserved for the reapers. He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, Matthew 13:24 but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. Matthew 13:25 So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. Matthew 13:26 And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?’ Matthew 13:27 He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ So the servants said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and gather them?’ Matthew 13:28 But he said, ‘No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. Matthew 13:29 Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” Matthew 13:30

title: Matthew 13:31–35
context: Jesus adds twin kingdom images—mustard seed and leaven—then Matthew explains His parable method as fulfillment of prophetic speech that utters what has been hidden.
text: Matthew 13:31–35 Matthew Jesus adds twin kingdom images—mustard seed and leaven—then Matthew explains His parable method as fulfillment of prophetic speech that utters what has been hidden. He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. Matthew 13:31 It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” Matthew 13:32 He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.” Matthew 13:33 All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. Matthew 13:34 This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” Matthew 13:35

title: Matthew 13:36–43
context: Leaving the crowds, Jesus enters the house and explains the weeds parable to the disciples: Son of Man, world-field, sons of kingdom and of the evil one, end-of-age harvest by angels, fiery judgment, and the righteous shining in the Father’s kingdom.
text: Matthew 13:36–43 Matthew Leaving the crowds, Jesus enters the house and explains the weeds parable to the disciples: Son of Man, world-field, sons of kingdom and of the evil one, end-of-age harvest by angels, fiery judgment, and the righteous shining in the Father’s kingdom. Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” Matthew 13:36 He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. Matthew 13:37 The field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, Matthew 13:38 and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. Matthew 13:39 Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. Matthew 13:40 The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers, Matthew 13:41 and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Matthew 13:42 Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear. Matthew 13:43

title: Matthew 13:44–46
context: Jesus pairs two brief kingdom images: treasure hidden in a field and a merchant finding one pearl of great value—both ending in joyful, total exchange for what is found.
text: Matthew 13:44–46 Matthew Jesus pairs two brief kingdom images: treasure hidden in a field and a merchant finding one pearl of great value—both ending in joyful, total exchange for what is found. “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Matthew 13:44 “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, Matthew 13:45 who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Matthew 13:46

title: Matthew 13:47–52
context: Jesus adds the dragnet parable of final separation, then asks whether the disciples understand and compares the trained kingdom scribe to a householder bringing out new and old treasure.
text: Matthew 13:47–52 Matthew Jesus adds the dragnet parable of final separation, then asks whether the disciples understand and compares the trained kingdom scribe to a householder bringing out new and old treasure. “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. Matthew 13:47 When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. Matthew 13:48 So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous Matthew 13:49 and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Matthew 13:50 “Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” Matthew 13:51 And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” Matthew 13:52

title: Matthew 13:53–58
context: After the parable discourse, Jesus returns to His hometown synagogue. Familiarity breeds offense: neighbors name His family, stumble over His wisdom and works, and unbelief limits the mighty works done there.
text: Matthew 13:53–58 Matthew After the parable discourse, Jesus returns to His hometown synagogue. Familiarity breeds offense: neighbors name His family, stumble over His wisdom and works, and unbelief limits the mighty works done there. And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there, Matthew 13:53 and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Matthew 13:54 Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? Matthew 13:55 And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?” Matthew 13:56 And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” Matthew 13:57 And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief. Matthew 13:58

title: Matthew 14:1–12
context: After Nazareth’s unbelief closes Matthew 13, the narrative turns to Herod Antipas: rumors of Jesus’ fame reopen the story of John’s imprisonment and beheading. The flashback ends as John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus—immediately before the feeding of the five thousand.
text: Matthew 14:1–12 Matthew After Nazareth’s unbelief closes Matthew 13, the narrative turns to Herod Antipas: rumors of Jesus’ fame reopen the story of John’s imprisonment and beheading. The flashback ends as John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus—immediately before the feeding of the five thousand. At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, Matthew 14:1 and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” Matthew 14:2 For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, Matthew 14:3 because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” Matthew 14:4 And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. Matthew 14:5 But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod, Matthew 14:6 so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Matthew 14:7 Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” Matthew 14:8 And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. Matthew 14:9 He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, Matthew 14:10 and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. Matthew 14:11 And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. Matthew 14:12

title: Matthew 14:13–21
context: After John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus (14:1–12), Jesus withdraws by boat to a desolate place—yet the crowds follow on foot. Evening brings the disciples’ scarcity report, five loaves and two fish placed in His hands, a blessing, broken bread, satisfied multitudes, and twelve baskets left over.
text: Matthew 14:13–21 Matthew After John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus (14:1–12), Jesus withdraws by boat to a desolate place—yet the crowds follow on foot. Evening brings the disciples’ scarcity report, five loaves and two fish placed in His hands, a blessing, broken bread, satisfied multitudes, and twelve baskets left over. Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. Matthew 14:13 When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. Matthew 14:14 Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” Matthew 14:15 But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” Matthew 14:16 They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” Matthew 14:17 And he said, “Bring them here to me.” Matthew 14:18 Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. Matthew 14:19 And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Matthew 14:20 And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. Matthew 14:21

title: Matthew 14:22–33
context: After the five thousand eat and twelve baskets remain (14:13–21), Jesus immediately sends the disciples ahead by boat, dismisses the crowds, and prays alone on the mountain. In the night storm He walks on the sea, steadies their fear—“It is I”—receives Peter’s venture of faith, rescues him when fear sinks him, stills the wind, and hears the boat’s worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”
text: Matthew 14:22–33 Matthew After the five thousand eat and twelve baskets remain (14:13–21), Jesus immediately sends the disciples ahead by boat, dismisses the crowds, and prays alone on the mountain. In the night storm He walks on the sea, steadies their fear—“It is I”—receives Peter’s venture of faith, rescues him when fear sinks him, stills the wind, and hears the boat’s worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.” Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. Matthew 14:22 And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, Matthew 14:23 but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. Matthew 14:24 And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. Matthew 14:25 But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear. Matthew 14:26 But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” Matthew 14:27 And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” Matthew 14:28 He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. Matthew 14:29 But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” Matthew 14:30 Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” Matthew 14:31 And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. Matthew 14:32 And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” Matthew 14:33

title: Matthew 14:34–36
context: After the storm stills and the disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God (14:22–33), they land at Gennesaret. Recognition spreads through the region: the sick are brought, the fringe of His garment is sought, and all who touch are made well—mercy continuing on shore after glory on the sea.
text: Matthew 14:34–36 Matthew After the storm stills and the disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God (14:22–33), they land at Gennesaret. Recognition spreads through the region: the sick are brought, the fringe of His garment is sought, and all who touch are made well—mercy continuing on shore after glory on the sea. And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. Matthew 14:34 And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick Matthew 14:35 and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well. Matthew 14:36

title: Matthew 15:1–9
context: Pharisees and scribes arrive from Jerusalem and accuse Jesus’ disciples of breaking the tradition of the elders by eating with unwashed hands. Jesus turns the charge: their Corban practice voids God’s command to honor father and mother, and Isaiah’s word exposes lip-service worship that teaches human commandments as doctrine.
text: Matthew 15:1–9 Matthew Pharisees and scribes arrive from Jerusalem and accuse Jesus’ disciples of breaking the tradition of the elders by eating with unwashed hands. Jesus turns the charge: their Corban practice voids God’s command to honor father and mother, and Isaiah’s word exposes lip-service worship that teaches human commandments as doctrine. Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, Matthew 15:1 “Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” Matthew 15:2 He answered them, “And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? Matthew 15:3 For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ Matthew 15:4 But you say, ‘If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God,” Matthew 15:5 he need not honor his father.’ So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. Matthew 15:6 You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: Matthew 15:7 “‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; Matthew 15:8 in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” Matthew 15:9

title: Matthew 15:10–20
context: Jesus turns from the Jerusalem challengers to the crowd: defilement is not what enters the mouth but what comes out of it. When the disciples report Pharisaic offense, He speaks of unplanted plants, blind guides, and—answering Peter—evil that proceeds from the heart. Unwashed hands do not defile; the heart’s overflow does.
text: Matthew 15:10–20 Matthew Jesus turns from the Jerusalem challengers to the crowd: defilement is not what enters the mouth but what comes out of it. When the disciples report Pharisaic offense, He speaks of unplanted plants, blind guides, and—answering Peter—evil that proceeds from the heart. Unwashed hands do not defile; the heart’s overflow does. And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand: Matthew 15:10 it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person.” Matthew 15:11 Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” Matthew 15:12 He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Matthew 15:13 Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” Matthew 15:14 But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” Matthew 15:15 And he said, “Are you also still without understanding? Matthew 15:16 Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? Matthew 15:17 But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person. Matthew 15:18 For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. Matthew 15:19 These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.” Matthew 15:20

title: Matthew 15:21–28
context: Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman cries for mercy to the Son of David for her demon-oppressed daughter. After silence, a word about Israel’s lost sheep, and a hard saying about children’s bread, her faith answers with crumbs from the masters’ table. Jesus praises her great faith; her daughter is healed instantly.
text: Matthew 15:21–28 Matthew Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman cries for mercy to the Son of David for her demon-oppressed daughter. After silence, a word about Israel’s lost sheep, and a hard saying about children’s bread, her faith answers with crumbs from the masters’ table. Jesus praises her great faith; her daughter is healed instantly. And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. Matthew 15:21 And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.” Matthew 15:22 But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” Matthew 15:23 He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Matthew 15:24 But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.” Matthew 15:25 And he answered, “It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs.” Matthew 15:26 She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.” Matthew 15:27 Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed instantly. Matthew 15:28

title: Matthew 15:29–39
context: From the coast Jesus returns beside the Sea of Galilee, sits on the mountain, and heals crowds of lame, blind, crippled, mute, and many others; they glorify the God of Israel. He then has compassion on a three-day crowd with nothing to eat, multiplies seven loaves and a few fish, satisfies about four thousand men besides women and children, gathers seven baskets of leftovers, and departs by boat to the region of Magadan.
text: Matthew 15:29–39 Matthew From the coast Jesus returns beside the Sea of Galilee, sits on the mountain, and heals crowds of lame, blind, crippled, mute, and many others; they glorify the God of Israel. He then has compassion on a three-day crowd with nothing to eat, multiplies seven loaves and a few fish, satisfies about four thousand men besides women and children, gathers seven baskets of leftovers, and departs by boat to the region of Magadan. Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. Matthew 15:29 And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them, Matthew 15:30 so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. Matthew 15:31 Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” Matthew 15:32 And the disciples said to him, “Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?” Matthew 15:33 And Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” Matthew 15:34 And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, Matthew 15:35 he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. Matthew 15:36 And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Matthew 15:37 Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. Matthew 15:38 And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan. Matthew 15:39

title: Matthew 16:1–4
context: After feeding multitudes and healing, Jesus is confronted by Pharisees and Sadducees who demand a sign from heaven. He exposes their spiritual blindness, refuses a spectacle, and points them to the sign of Jonah—then leaves them.
text: Matthew 16:1–4 Matthew After feeding multitudes and healing, Jesus is confronted by Pharisees and Sadducees who demand a sign from heaven. He exposes their spiritual blindness, refuses a spectacle, and points them to the sign of Jonah—then leaves them. And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. Matthew 16:1 He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ Matthew 16:2 And in the morning, ‘It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. Matthew 16:3 An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” So he left them and departed. Matthew 16:4

title: Matthew 16:13–20
