Romans 8:23 For in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? Romans 8:24 But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. Romans 8:25 Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. Romans 8:26 And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God. Romans 8:27 And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. Romans 8:28 For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Romans 8:29 And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. Romans 8:30

title: Romans 8:31–39
context: After the golden chain, Paul asks who can be against us, who will bring a charge, who will separate us from the love of Christ: tribulation, death, life, angels, nothing in all creation.
text: Romans 8:31–39 Romans After the golden chain, Paul asks who can be against us, who will bring a charge, who will separate us from the love of Christ: tribulation, death, life, angels, nothing in all creation. What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? Romans 8:31 He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? Romans 8:32 Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Romans 8:33 Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us. Romans 8:34 Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? Romans 8:35 As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.” Romans 8:36 No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. Romans 8:37 For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, Romans 8:38 nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Romans 8:39

title: Romans 9:1–13
context: Paul’s grief for Israel names the covenants and Christ according to the flesh; yet not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel: the children of promise, not of the flesh, are counted as offspring—Jacob and Esau before they were born, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
text: Romans 9:1–13 Romans Paul’s grief for Israel names the covenants and Christ according to the flesh; yet not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel: the children of promise, not of the flesh, are counted as offspring—Jacob and Esau before they were born, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit— Romans 9:1 that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. Romans 9:2 For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh. Romans 9:3 They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises. Romans 9:4 To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen. Romans 9:5 But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, Romans 9:6 and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” Romans 9:7 This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring. Romans 9:8 For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.” Romans 9:9 And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac, Romans 9:10 though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls— Romans 9:11 she was told, “The older will serve the younger.” Romans 9:12 As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Romans 9:13

title: Romans 9:14–29
context: After Jacob and Esau, Paul answers the charge of injustice on God’s part with Moses and Pharaoh, the potter’s right over the clay, vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy, a remnant saved, and Gentiles called.
text: Romans 9:14–29 Romans After Jacob and Esau, Paul answers the charge of injustice on God’s part with Moses and Pharaoh, the potter’s right over the clay, vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy, a remnant saved, and Gentiles called. What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means! Romans 9:14 For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Romans 9:15 So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. Romans 9:16 For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” Romans 9:17 So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. Romans 9:18 You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” Romans 9:19 But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” Romans 9:20 Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use? Romans 9:21 What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, Romans 9:22 in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory— Romans 9:23 even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles? Romans 9:24 As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved.’” Romans 9:25 “And in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’” Romans 9:26 And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, Romans 9:27 for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.” Romans 9:28 And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.” Romans 9:29

title: Romans 9:30–33
context: Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained it by faith; Israel who pursued a law of righteousness did not succeed, because they did not pursue by faith but as if it were based on works; they stumbled over the stumbling stone.
text: Romans 9:30–33 Romans Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained it by faith; Israel who pursued a law of righteousness did not succeed, because they did not pursue by faith but as if it were based on works; they stumbled over the stumbling stone. What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; Romans 9:30 but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law. Romans 9:31 Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, Romans 9:32 as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” Romans 9:33

title: Titus 1:1–4
context: Paul greets Titus as his true child in a common faith, naming himself a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness. Eternal life was promised by the God who never lies before the ages began, and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching entrusted to Paul by the command of God our Savior.
text: Titus 1:1–4 Titus Paul greets Titus as his true child in a common faith, naming himself a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness. Eternal life was promised by the God who never lies before the ages began, and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching entrusted to Paul by the command of God our Savior. Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, Titus 1:1 in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began Titus 1:2 and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior; Titus 1:3 To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior. Titus 1:4

title: Titus 1:10–16
context: The reason for such elders: many are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision party, upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not. A Cretan prophet said Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons; the testimony is true, so rebuke them sharply that they may be sound in the faith, not devoted to Jewish myths and human commands. To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is; they profess to know God but deny him by their works.
text: Titus 1:10–16 Titus The reason for such elders: many are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision party, upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not. A Cretan prophet said Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons; the testimony is true, so rebuke them sharply that they may be sound in the faith, not devoted to Jewish myths and human commands. To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is; they profess to know God but deny him by their works. For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. Titus 1:10 They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach. Titus 1:11 One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” Titus 1:12 This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, Titus 1:13 not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. Titus 1:14 To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled. Titus 1:15 They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work. Titus 1:16

title: Titus 1:5–9
context: Paul left Titus in Crete to put what remained into order and appoint elders in every town: men above reproach, the husband of one wife, with believing children not open to debauchery or insubordination. An overseer, as God’s steward, must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent, or greedy, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined, holding firm the trustworthy word so as to instruct in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it.
text: Titus 1:5–9 Titus Paul left Titus in Crete to put what remained into order and appoint elders in every town: men above reproach, the husband of one wife, with believing children not open to debauchery or insubordination. An overseer, as God’s steward, must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent, or greedy, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined, holding firm the trustworthy word so as to instruct in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it. This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— Titus 1:5 if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination. Titus 1:6 For an overseer, as God’s steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, Titus 1:7 but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. Titus 1:8 He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it. Titus 1:9

title: Titus 2:1–8
context: Paul turns from Crete’s empty talkers to the life that matches sound doctrine: older men; older women who train the young women in household love and order; younger men; and Titus himself as a visible pattern. The public aim is that the word of God may not be reviled and that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say.
text: Titus 2:1–8 Titus Paul turns from Crete’s empty talkers to the life that matches sound doctrine: older men; older women who train the young women in household love and order; younger men; and Titus himself as a visible pattern. The public aim is that the word of God may not be reviled and that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say. But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Titus 2:1 Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. Titus 2:2 Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good, Titus 2:3 and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, Titus 2:4 to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled. Titus 2:5 Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Titus 2:6 Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, Titus 2:7 and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us. Titus 2:8

title: Titus 2:11–15
context: The household charges rest on a gospel: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and to live godly lives while we wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us and to purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works. Titus must declare these things with authority.
text: Titus 2:11–15 Titus The household charges rest on a gospel: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and to live godly lives while we wait for the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us and to purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works. Titus must declare these things with authority. For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, Titus 2:11 training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, Titus 2:12 waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, Titus 2:13 who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Titus 2:14 Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you. Titus 2:15

title: Titus 2:9–10
context: Paul continues the household counsel: bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters, well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, showing all good faith—so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. The aim is the gospel’s public beauty in a first-century yoke, not a theory of the institution.
text: Titus 2:9–10 Titus Paul continues the household counsel: bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters, well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, showing all good faith—so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. The aim is the gospel’s public beauty in a first-century yoke, not a theory of the institution. Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, Titus 2:9 not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. Titus 2:10

title: Titus 3:1–8
context: Titus is to remind the church of civic gentleness and courtesy toward all people, because we ourselves were once foolish and enslaved. The turn is mercy: when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, He saved us, not by works, but according to mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that being justified by His grace we might become heirs. Those who have believed are to devote themselves to good works.
text: Titus 3:1–8 Titus Titus is to remind the church of civic gentleness and courtesy toward all people, because we ourselves were once foolish and enslaved. The turn is mercy: when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, He saved us, not by works, but according to mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that being justified by His grace we might become heirs. Those who have believed are to devote themselves to good works. Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, Titus 3:1 to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people. Titus 3:2 For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another. Titus 3:3 But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, Titus 3:4 he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, Titus 3:5 whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, Titus 3:6 so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. Titus 3:7 The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people. Titus 3:8

title: Titus 3:9–15
context: After the trustworthy saying Paul fences the church: avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law; after a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a person who stirs up division. Travel plans, help for Zenas and Apollos, a charge that our people learn to devote themselves to good works, and a closing greeting and grace.
text: Titus 3:9–15 Titus After the trustworthy saying Paul fences the church: avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law; after a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a person who stirs up division. Travel plans, help for Zenas and Apollos, a charge that our people learn to devote themselves to good works, and a closing greeting and grace. But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. Titus 3:9 As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, Titus 3:10 knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned. Titus 3:11 When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Titus 3:12 Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. Titus 3:13 And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful. Titus 3:14 All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all. Titus 3:15

title: Election
context: Before the foundation of the world, God chose a people in Christ to be holy and blameless—both camps read that choosing as grace, and they part over whether it is conditional on foreseen faith.
text: Election Before the foundation of the world, God chose a people in Christ to be holy and blameless—both camps read that choosing as grace, and they part over whether it is conditional on foreseen faith. Election is the church’s word for God’s choosing. Scripture praises the Father who “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” and names “God’s elect.” Arminian and Reformed readers agree the praise belongs to God, not to human merit. They disagree about the ground of the choice: God’s foreknowledge of a grace-enabled response, or God’s unconditional good pleasure that itself creates faith. Arminian readings typically make foreseen, grace-enabled faith (or entry into the elect body in Christ) the difference between the chosen and the rest; Reformed readings make God’s unconditional choice the difference, with faith as the effectual result.

title: Atonement
context: Christ died as a real sacrifice for sin—both camps preach a cross of infinite worth; they part over whether the Father intended that death for every person or for the elect in particular.
text: Atonement Christ died as a real sacrifice for sin—both camps preach a cross of infinite worth; they part over whether the Father intended that death for every person or for the elect in particular. Atonement is the work by which the death of Jesus deals with guilt. Scripture calls him the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, a ransom, a propitiation, the one who lays down his life for the sheep. Arminian and Reformed teachers agree the cross is substitutionary in some real sense and that no one is saved apart from it. They disagree about the design: a sufficient provision for all, applied to believers, or a particular redemption that infallibly secures a people. Arminians typically teach a universal provision (every person’s sins remissible) applied by resistible, enabling grace through faith; the Reformed typically teach a particular design that infallibly obtains faith and salvation for the elect, while still confessing the infinite worth of the death and a real gospel offer.

title: Justification
context: God counts the believer righteous for Christ’s sake—both camps preach pardon and acceptance by grace through faith; they part over how faith relates to election, and whether the justified can fall from that standing.
text: Justification God counts the believer righteous for Christ’s sake—both camps preach pardon and acceptance by grace through faith; they part over how faith relates to election, and whether the justified can fall from that standing. Justification is God’s verdict that a sinner is in the right with him. Genesis 15, “Abraham believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness,” and the later apostolic gospel of grace not works sit at the center. Arminius and the magisterial Reformers were closer here than popular debate suggests: both spoke of imputation and faith. The live forks are whether justifying faith is itself the effect of unconditional election, and whether the verdict can be lost. Both camps preach justification by grace through faith on the ground of Christ. Arminians typically treat believing as a resistible, grace-enabled condition that must continue; the Reformed typically treat faith as the instrumental effect of God’s prior, effectual mercy, and the verdict as final for those in Christ.

title: Regeneration
context: The Spirit makes the dead alive in Christ—both camps preach a real new birth, not mere turning over a new leaf; they part over whether that birth can be resisted, and whether it precedes faith or is given with it.
text: Regeneration The Spirit makes the dead alive in Christ—both camps preach a real new birth, not mere turning over a new leaf; they part over whether that birth can be resisted, and whether it precedes faith or is given with it. Regeneration is new birth: God raising a person from spiritual death. Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born from above; Paul says we were dead in trespasses and God made us alive; Titus names the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. The shared confession is that fallen people need a work God does in us, not only a message we approve. The fork is the mode: irresistible new creation, or a birth bound up with a grace that can be refused. Both preach a Spirit-wrought new creation. Arminians typically bind new birth to resistible, enabling grace and to faith as a real response; the Reformed typically treat regeneration as an effectual, supernatural raising that produces faith rather than waiting on it.

title: Perseverance
context: Those in Christ are called to abide, and God is faithful—both camps take the warnings and the promises as real; they part over whether a true believer can finally fall away.
text: Perseverance Those in Christ are called to abide, and God is faithful—both camps take the warnings and the promises as real; they part over whether a true believer can finally fall away. Perseverance names the question: will those who have believed be kept to the end? Jesus speaks of branches in the vine that are cut off, of sheep who will never perish, of disciples who walk away. Paul endures “for the sake of the elect,” quotes a trustworthy saying about dying and living with Christ, and names Demas who loved this present world. Arminian and Reformed readers both refuse cheap grace. They disagree whether the warnings describe the ruin of the truly regenerate, or the means by which God keeps his own. Arminians typically teach that a truly regenerate believer may finally fall by ceasing to believe; the Reformed typically teach that those whom God has accepted and called will be preserved—warnings included as means—so that apostasy proves a faith that was not saving.

title: Holiness
context: God is the Holy One—utterly pure, set apart, and worthy of fear and love—and both camps call his people to be holy as he is holy.
text: Holiness God is the Holy One—utterly pure, set apart, and worthy of fear and love—and both camps call his people to be holy as he is holy. Holiness names God’s moral purity and his being set apart. Seraphim cry “holy” ; the Father is perfect; the man of God is told to pursue righteousness and to keep the commandment unstained. Arminian and Reformed teachers do not disagree that God is holy. They disagree about how that holiness meets a sinful world: whether holy love makes a provision for all, and whether holy justice requires a particular satisfaction for a chosen people. The verses still come first. Both confess the Holy One and the call to be holy. Arminians typically unfold holiness as perfect love that sincerely seeks all; the Reformed typically unfold holiness as infinite purity that includes a justice satisfied in a particular, effectual redemption—without denying the call to holiness of life.

title: Love
context: God is love, and he has loved in the sending of the Son—both camps refuse a loveless God; they part over whether that love, in the design of salvation, is for every person or particularly for the elect.
text: Love God is love, and he has loved in the sending of the Son—both camps refuse a loveless God; they part over whether that love, in the design of salvation, is for every person or particularly for the elect. Love is not a soft extra in God. Jesus names the Father’s love for the world, for the disciples, and for those who will believe through their word. The two great commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets. Paul blesses the God who chose us in love and kneels to pray that believers may know love that surpasses knowledge. The shared confession: God loves. The live fork is the scope of saving love—world as all persons, or world as the elect in the world—and whether love can be refused. Arminians typically read God’s saving love as sincere toward every person and resistible in its grace; the Reformed typically confess a real invitation to all and a particular, effectual love that actually saves the elect—without meaning that God is unloving toward the world he has made.

title: Justice
context: God is righteous—wrath against sin is real, and he will by no means clear the guilty—and both camps confess it; they part over how that justice orders mercy, not over whether judgment is a mood.
text: Justice God is righteous—wrath against sin is real, and he will by no means clear the guilty—and both camps confess it; they part over how that justice orders mercy, not over whether judgment is a mood. Justice is God’s rectitude. Wrath is revealed from heaven against ungodliness; God shows no partiality; he is just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus; Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will do what is right; Belshazzar is weighed and found wanting; the Son of Man separates sheep and goats. This hub is not the atonement hub, though it may point there. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a soft God who never judges. The live fork is how justice and mercy meet—terms fixed for all who believe, or a particular satisfaction for a chosen people. The verses still come first. Both confess that God is righteous and that wrath against sin is real. Arminians typically unfold justice as the published terms of mercy to all who believe; the Reformed typically unfold justice as a rectitude God would owe to none, often satisfied in a particular redemption—without either camp denying the coming judgment.

title: Mercy
context: Mercy is God’s pity toward the miserable—not a second name for the love hub—and both camps confess it; they part over Romans 9’s “I will have mercy,” whether it names whom he wills or a sincere general mercy with particular application.
text: Mercy Mercy is God’s pity toward the miserable—not a second name for the love hub—and both camps confess it; they part over Romans 9’s “I will have mercy,” whether it names whom he wills or a sincere general mercy with particular application. Mercy is pity toward the miserable. Paul says God is rich in mercy; he saved us according to his mercy; Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul obtained mercy; Daniel pleads, we do not present our pleas because of our righteousness but because of your great mercy. The Beatitudes open with the merciful. This page is not the love hub. Love is God’s affection and self-giving; mercy is that love meeting misery and guilt. Both camps refuse a God without pity. Romans 9 is the real fork: mercy on whom he wills, or mercy offered on published terms to all who will receive it. The verses still come first. Both confess mercy as pity toward the miserable, distinct from the love hub. Arminians typically read Romans 9 as God’s right to fix terms of mercy for all who believe; the Reformed typically read it as free pity that is not given to all indiscriminately, while still sending the Son that whoever believes should not perish.

title: Faithfulness
context: God keeps covenant—if we are faithless, he remains faithful—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that his word cannot fail, though they may differ over whom the promises finally hold.
text: Faithfulness God keeps covenant—if we are faithless, he remains faithful—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that his word cannot fail, though they may differ over whom the promises finally hold. Faithfulness is God’s covenant-keeping. He remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself; Jewish unbelief does not nullify the faithfulness of God; Abraham was fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised; he is faithful and just to forgive; he sets his bow in the cloud; he cuts a covenant with Abram; Daniel pleads the covenant and steadfast love. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a God who forgets his word. The verses still come first. Any fork is usually about the scope of the promise, not about whether God is true. Both confess that God keeps covenant and that unbelief does not make him a liar. Arminians typically stress that he remains faithful and still makes good the promise to those who believe; the Reformed typically stress that his verity does not depend on us and that the covenant retains its power toward those he has given to the Son.

title: Omnipotence
context: God can do all that is consistent with his nature—both camps confess the Almighty, and neither treats power as a magic that lies, un-Gods himself, or authors sin.
text: Omnipotence God can do all that is consistent with his nature—both camps confess the Almighty, and neither treats power as a magic that lies, un-Gods himself, or authors sin. Omnipotence is not a blank check. Scripture’s first word is that God created; the Lord asks Abraham whether anything is too hard; Jesus says that with God all things are possible; Nebuchadnezzar learns that none can stay the Most High’s hand. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a weak God and a magical God who can contradict himself. The live question is not whether God is able, but how that ability relates to creaturely will and the origin of sin. The verses still come first. Both confess that God can do all that is consistent with his nature. Arminians typically refuse to let that power author sin or make saving grace irresistible; the Reformed typically unfold omnipotence as actual, particular government—including who is effectually drawn—without meaning that God does evil.

title: Omniscience
context: God knows all things—himself, the possible, and the actual—and classical Arminians are not open theists; both camps confess exhaustive knowledge and part over how that knowledge relates to the decree.
text: Omniscience God knows all things—himself, the possible, and the actual—and classical Arminians are not open theists; both camps confess exhaustive knowledge and part over how that knowledge relates to the decree. Omniscience is not a guess that improves with time. Jesus knows what is in man; the Father knows what we need before we ask; the Spirit will declare the things that are to come; Paul bows before knowledge too deep to track. Arminius and Wesley, no less than Calvin and Westminster, refuse a God who learns. The live fork is not whether God is ignorant, but whether his knowledge of future free acts is grounded in an unconditional decree, or whether—sometimes with middle knowledge—he knows what creatures would and will do without that knowledge itself causing the act. The verses still come first. Both confess that God knows all things, including future free acts; classical Arminians are not open theists. Arminians typically deny that knowledge itself causes those acts (sometimes via middle knowledge); the Reformed typically deny that God decreed because he foresaw, locating certainty in a counsel independent of the creature.

title: Omnipresence
context: God is wholly present everywhere—not spread thin, not locked in a shrine—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Father, the risen Christ, and the Spirit are with the church.
text: Omnipresence God is wholly present everywhere—not spread thin, not locked in a shrine—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Father, the risen Christ, and the Spirit are with the church. Omnipresence is God’s immensity meeting the world he made. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when worship will not be tied to this mountain or that; he promises to be in the midst of two or three and to be with his disciples to the end of the age. Jacob wakes and says the Lord is in this place. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a local God and a pantheist smear of God into the furniture. The verses still come first. Any fork is pastoral more than confessional: how nearness comforts, convicts, and orders worship—not whether God is here. Both confess that God is wholly present everywhere and is not confined to temples. There is no historic Arminian–Reformed split on the attribute itself; any remaining difference belongs to how that near God applies saving grace, not to whether he is here.

title: Immutability
context: God does not change in being or character—both camps confess it, and both read “relented” texts as a change of dealing, not a mutable essence; prayer is not wasted.
text: Immutability God does not change in being or character—both camps confess it, and both read “relented” texts as a change of dealing, not a mutable essence; prayer is not wasted. Immutability is God’s sameness. He remains faithful; he cannot deny himself; the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable; he is light without darkness. Genesis 6’s “it grieved him” is in the same Bible. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a God who grows, learns, or improves, and both refuse a frozen God who cannot answer prayer. They handle relenting language the same way in substance: anthropomorphism and a real change of treatment, not a change of essence. The verses still come first. Both confess that God does not change in being or character, and both read relenting texts as a change of dealing rather than a mutable essence. Prayer is not wasted. Any remaining fork is whether an unchanging counsel includes resistible grace, not whether God is still becoming.

title: Eternity
context: God is without beginning or end—the King of the ages—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Word was in the beginning, or that immortality belongs to God.
text: Eternity God is without beginning or end—the King of the ages—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Word was in the beginning, or that immortality belongs to God. Eternity is not merely a long time. Paul blesses the King of the ages, immortal and invisible; he speaks of the blessed and only Sovereign who alone has immortality; John opens with the Word who was in the beginning; Genesis opens with God already there when time starts. Nebuchadnezzar learns that God’s dominion is everlasting. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a God who came to be, and both refuse to treat “eternal” as a mood. The verses still come first. Any fork is almost none on the attribute itself. Both confess that God is without beginning or end and that the Word was in the beginning. There is no historic split on the attribute itself; remaining disagreement belongs to how an eternal purpose relates to election, not to whether God is everlasting.

title: Sovereignty
context: God rules; nothing is finally outside his hand—both camps confess a King, and they part over whether that rule includes an unconditional decree of who will believe.
text: Sovereignty God rules; nothing is finally outside his hand—both camps confess a King, and they part over whether that rule includes an unconditional decree of who will believe. Sovereignty is God’s kingly right and actual rule. Scripture blesses the God who works all things according to the counsel of his will, the Father who draws, the Lord of the wedding feast, the blessed and only Sovereign. Arminian and Reformed Christians both reject a God who cannot save and a world of pure chance. They disagree whether sovereignty means that God determines the outcome of every human choice in salvation, or that he governs in ways that leave a grace-enabled refusal possible. Both confess that God rules. Arminians typically describe a sovereignty that eternally purposes to save believers and governs without irresistible determination of the will; the Reformed typically describe a sovereignty that ordains whatsoever comes to pass—including who will be effectually drawn—without making God the author of sin.
